title: Presence of MET exon 14 skipping and fusion as mechanism of osimertinb resistance in a lung adenocarcinoma with an EGFR exon 19 deletion that responds to combination of capmatinib and osimertinb: A case report
author: Siqi Xiang; Liang Zeng; Mingjun Xiang; Yongchang Zhang
text:
Abstract
Lung cancer stands as a leading cause of mortality in China, with EGFR mutations frequently identified as pivotal driver genes. Osimertinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting EGFR mutations, is typically employed as a first-line treatment for EGFR-sensitive mutations; nevertheless, resistance can emerge. In this case report, we present the case of a 53-year-old non-smoking male diagnosed with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma bearing an EGFR exon 19 deletion. This patient eventually developed resistance to both Erlotinib and Osimertinib after 28 months of treatment. Subsequent genetic testing uncovered the emergence of new MET exon 14 skipping and MET fusion, coexisting with the initial EGFR exon 19 deletion. In light of this complex molecular profile, the patient was administered a combination therapy consisting of Osimertinib and Capmatinib. This novel approach yielded a partial response, and notably, the patient experienced a progression-free survival exceeding 7 months. Vigilant monitoring of the patient's progress revealed the disappearance of the MET exon 14 skipping and a notable improvement in the patient's symptoms. This case report underscores the potential efficacy of Osimertinib and Capmatinib combination therapy as a viable treatment strategy for patients harboring EGFR-mutated lung cancer who develop resistance to first-line EGFR inhibitors due to MET activation.
Keywords: MET exon 14 skipping, MET fusion, Resistance mechanism, Osimertinib, Capmatinib, EGFR, NSCLC
1. Introduction
In China, lung cancer holds the dubious distinction of having the highest incidence and mortality rates [1]. Among the numerous driver genes in lung cancer, EGFR mutations are the most prevalent. Extensive research has demonstrated that Osimertinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting EGFR mutations,has been found to help extends the progression-free survival and overall survival of lung cancer patients with EGFR-sensitive mutations [2]. However, the development of resistance is an inevitable challenge.
Capmatinib, an oral agent belonging to the highly selective class Ib c-MET inhibitors, presents a promising solution. In vitro experiments have revealed that Capmatinib boasts an exceptional IC50 and exerts robust inhibitory effects against c-MET targets, surpassing other MET inhibitors by a factor of 30 compared to clotozantinib and 5 times compared to Tepotinib. The Global Multicenter Registered Clinical Study GEOMETRY mono-1 [3], encompassing 9 trial groups, investigates the efficacy and safety of Capmatinib for METex14 skipping and MET amplification. Among these, Cohorts 5b and 7 corroborated the first-line effectiveness and safety of Capmatinib in METex14 skipping NSCLC patients. The outcomes were remarkable, with a first-line ORR of 68.3 %, a median PFS of 12.5 months, and an impressive median OS of 25.5 months, positioning it as the leading MET inhibitor. Validation between Cohorts 4 and 6 demonstrated a second-line ORR of 44 %, with a median duration of response (mDoR) at 9.7 months and a median PFS at 5.5 months.
Capmatinib's outstanding performance led to its FDA accelerated approval being upgraded to regular approval in August 2022, making it the sole METex14 skipping inhibitor with such recognition. Further biomarker exploration unveiled that the depth and duration of lesion remission induced by Capmatinib remained consistent regardless of the type of MET mutation/amplification. Notably, Capmatinib has shown remarkable efficacy in treating brain metastases. In the GEOMETRY mono-1 study, 7 out of 13 patients with brain lesions exhibited intracranial responses upon initial evaluation, with complete resolution of all brain lesions in 4 patients. Ultimately, 12 patients achieved intracranial lesion control (92.3 %). A real-world study, published in ASCO in 2022, confirmed a high intracranial disease control rate (iDCR) of 96.4 % within the Capmatinib group, further substantiating its outstanding intracranial efficacy.
Osimertinib resistance mechanisms encompass C797S and various bypass activations, including MET amplification [4], with subsequent treatment plans posing significant challenges. We present a case of advanced lung cancer with an EGFR exon 19 deletion mutation that developed resistance to Erlotinib and Osimertinib. Genetic testing unveiled MET exon 14 skipping and MET fusion. Following a regimen of Osimertinib and Capmatinib combination therapy, the lesions rapidly regressed and sustained remission for over a year.
1.1. Case presentation
In March 2018, a 53-year-old Chinese man, a lifelong non-smoker, presented with persistent chest tightness and pain. CT scans revealed multiple small lung nodules in the right lower lobe, and a subsequent biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR exon 19 deletion (Fig. 1). The patient commenced first-line treatment with Erlotinib at a daily dose of 150 mg, resulting in a partial response (PR) as the tumors regressed. However, after 28 months, the patient's condition deteriorated, characterized by primary tumor enlargement and the emergence of new bone metastases. A biopsy confirmed the presence of both EGFR exon 19 deletion and the T790 M mutation.
The treatment approach was subsequently modified to oral Osimertinib at a daily dose of 80 mg, leading to a PR with a duration of 15.4 months (Fig. 1). However, further assessments indicated progressive disease (PD), characterized by new bone metastases and primary tumor enlargement. Next-generation sequencing identified the presence of new MET exon 14 skipping (c.3027_3028 + 21delAGGTATATTTCAGTTTATTGTTC) and MET fusion (EX13:EX15), in addition to the coexistence of EGFR exon 19 deletion (Fig. 2A–C, Table 1)

To address this complex molecular profile, the patient commenced a combination therapy regimen consisting of Osimertinib (80 mg, oral, daily) and Capmatinib (400 mg, oral, twice daily). This approach yielded a partial response with a manageable toxicity profile and a progression-free survival exceeding 7 months (Fig. 1A). Subsequent examinations revealed the disappearance of the MET exon 14 skipping, and the patient reported an improvement in symptoms such as coughing and expectoration. Additionally, the dual-target therapy effectively controlled the clinical condition of bone metastasis. The healthcare team maintained close monitoring of the patient's progress, ensuring that he received the appropriate treatment and support.
This case report highlights the potential efficacy of a combination therapy approach involving Osimertinib and Capmatinib in patients with EGFR-mutated lung cancer who develop resistance to initial EGFR inhibitors due to MET activation.
2. Discussion
Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comprises approximately 85 % of all lung cancer cases, with adenocarcinoma being one of its subtypes, accounting for about 40 % of all cases. In approximately 15–20 % of lung adenocarcinomas, there are Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) mutations, which can be targeted using EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) [2]. However, despite initial responses to EGFR TKI therapy, nearly all patients with EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinoma eventually develop resistance to these drugs within 1–2 years of treatment.
One of the most common mechanisms of resistance to EGFR TKI therapy in EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinoma is the alteration of the MET signaling pathway [4]. MET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a crucial role in cell growth, survival, and migration. In lung cancer, MET activation is associated with increased tumor growth and resistance to EGFR TKI therapy [5]. MET activation can occur in several ways in EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinoma. One mechanism is the amplification of the MET gene, leading to increased MET protein expression, either as a primary event or after EGFR TKI therapy. Another mechanism is the activation of MET signaling by HGF (hepatocyte growth factor), the ligand for the MET receptor, which can be secreted by tumor cells or stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment [6].
MET pathway activation can trigger downstream signaling through the PI3K/AKT and MAPK pathways, promoting cell survival, proliferation, and migration. Additionally, MET activation can activate other pathways like the STAT3 pathway, further enhancing tumor growth and survival [7,8].
Presence of MET alterations have been associated with poorer prognosis in EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinoma patients and is considered a potential biomarker for predicting resistance to EGFR TKI therapy. Studies have shown that patients with EGFR mutant lung adenocarcinoma and MET alterations are less likely to respond to EGFR TKI therapy and have shorter progression-free survival compared to those without MET alterations [9].
Given the role of MET alterations in EGFR TKI resistance, various strategies have been developed to target the MET pathway in combination with EGFR TKIs. One approach is dual inhibition of both EGFR and MET, either through combination therapy with an EGFR TKI and a MET inhibitor or through the use of a single agent targeting both receptors, such as the MET/EGFR inhibitor, osimertinib [8]. Another strategy is combining EGFR TKI therapy with agents targeting downstream signaling pathways activated by MET, such as PI3K inhibitors or MEK inhibitors [10,11].
In our case, we detected coexistence of EGFR and MET mutations in the second drug-resistant biopsy sample. If capmatinib were used alone, it might not effectively inhibit the proliferation of EGFR-positive tumor cells. Therefore, we opted for combination treatment with osimertinib. In this case, first-line Erlotinib was followed by second-line Osimertinib, resistance occurred, and a new MET 14 skipping mutation was detected in the drug-resistant biopsy samples. The choice of combining Capmatinib or other inhibitors is still under exploration.
Currently, two highly accessible targeted drugs for treating METex14 mutations in China are capmatinib and savolitinib. Capmatinib has shown an objective response rate (ORR) of 68 % and 41 % for patients with METex14 mutations who have not been previously treated or have received first or second-line treatment, with median progression-free survival (PFS) of 12.4 months and 5.4 months, respectively. Following Savolitinib treatment, the ORR for the IRC evaluated tumor remission evaluable group and the entire population group were 49.2 % and 42.9 %, respectively. The median PFS of the entire population group was 6.8 months, and the median overall survival (OS) was 12.5 months. However, more clinical data and comparative studies are needed for confirmation. In our case, we chose Capmatinib in combination with Osimertinib and achieved favorable therapeutic outcomes.
In conclusion, we report the first detection of MET exon 14 skipping and MET fusion in a patient with osimertinib resistance. This patient achieved remission with osimertinib combined with capmatinib treatment. Our findings provide valuable evidence for the subsequent treatment of such patients.
